speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to
point out only one factor which I think should be considered by the government concerning instructions which may be given to those who are charged with the administration of the act. I have had my attention directed recently to a case in which a value of about $9,000-$9,552, I think, was the exact figure- was placed upon mortgaged premises by the soldier settlement valuator. The mortgage on the property is for $11,500, and it was suggested that it should be reduced to $7,500. payable over a period of ten years, and that the rate of interest should be reduced from five to four per cent. I desire to point out one principle which, I think, has been overlooked with respect to the administration of the act. Bankruptcy contemplates the liquidation of the assets of the insolvent and the distribution of the proceeds pro rata among his creditors. That is to be kept in mind as the real basis of all bankruptcy legislation-realization and distribution. We applied the general principle of bankruptcy to the farmers' creditors and afforded them relief on that basis, but obviously we did not contemplate realization. The difference between true bankruptcy and the application of the bankruptcy principle is to be found in the fact that, instead of realization, we contemplate the retention by the debtor of his premises; but we afford him an opportunity to pay his creditors the same rate on 
the dollar as though there were an attempted realization, the theory being that realization would be at such a low figure that any amount of money which might be paid to the creditors would be so small that it could be easily discharged and met by his continuing to occupy his farm and to make out of his operations sufficient money to pay the rate on the dollar that would be realized by a forced realization or liquidation of his property. When the act was passed we contemplated the application of a principle which, I submit, has been overlooked. It is a very simple one: First, one that is now recognized, that there should be insolvency; and, second, that we should, in arriving at values, keep in mind prospective as well as present-day values.

In the discussion of
this section last evening the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) took exception to some of the policies of the Canadian Broadcasing Corporation, and in so doing mades specific reference to a recent broadcast over the Columbia broadcasting system and the Canadian broadcasting system, in which I participated. The inference from the remarks of the hon. member, which I have read very carefully to-day, I think is both unfounded and unfair. May I just read the paragraph to which I refer:
When we as members of a free parliament start to discuss these matters points of order are raised, but the radio commission permit debates to be broadcast which are certainly objectionable to a large portion of the population of Ontario and some of the other prov-

Radio Broadcasting
inces. I have read a criticism that was made in the British House of Commons of such discussions. The hon. members for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and Essex East (Mr. Martin) spoke over the rado in a network linked up by the CBC with the NBC. I did not hear their addresses as I was on a train at the time. I read, however, with interest, their speeches on other matters.
They discussed what Mr. Cordell Hull said after the Brussels conference.
And so on. Then-and in my opinion this was much more serious-the hon. member for Broadview was followed by the right hon. Prime Minister, who said:
Mr. Chairman, I must say that X find myself very much in sympathy with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) in the remarks which he has just made. At the present time rve have been very careful not to discuss in this parliament the proceedings of other parliaments, and I believe that a rule which we find it advisable to observe here should also be observed by the commission in connection with broadcasts that may be made under its authority.
These are very critical times, as all hon. members of the house know, and as the citizens of the country generally know. In ordinary times we would not think of criticizing in this parliament the policies of a government or the proceedings of a parliament of another part of the British Empire. The policies of Great Britain, of Australia and New Zealand are their own policies, their own domestic affairs, and it is not for this parliament to say whether Liberals or Conservatives or the Labour party of Great Britain are right or wrong in what they are advocating.
So far as any policy relates to our own affairs, wre are at perfect liberty, of course, to discuss as fully as we please the effect of government policy.
May I point out that in the broadcast in question there was no reference to the policies of Great Britain or even to the policies of this parliament or this government. The broadcast related purely to an academic discussion of the value of the League of Nations. And may I go one step further and say this, that if in a broadcast in the Dominion of Canada in the interests of free discussion to are not to be permitted to discuss policies that are of domestic interest, the moulding of public opinion in Canada is going to be very seriously interfered with. I would also draw to the attention of the committee this fact, that if Mr. Ferguson of the Winnipeg Free Press and Doctor H. L. Stewart, who are commentators on behalf of the radio corporation of this countiy, are to be prevented from expressing their opinions in their commentaries, then I say that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should prohibit the pro-Chamberlain broadcasts from Great
Britain that are re-broadcast over this country. I have particular reference to the broadcasts of Mr. Beverley Baxter under private arrangements with the Canadian broadcasting chain. I am of opinion that it is in the best interests of Canada that our broadcasting corporation should endeavour to get before the Canadian people the various points of view expressed in Canada and elsewhere at this time, because it is necessary that our people shall be well informed regarding all aspects of our domestic and international affairs.
May I point out further that the foreign policy of the Chamberlain government in Great Britain, which, as I have said, in my opinion does not represent the real feelings of the British people, as the recent by-elections show, may involve this country in a serious situation. I have before me a speech of the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), made in this chamber on February 4, 1937, at a time when the house was discussing a resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). At that time the right hon. gentleman said:
In the constitutional position of Canada today neutrality would mean that an enemy of our king could be a friend of Canada; that we could trade with him during a war in which the king might be engaged; that to nations with which the king might be at war we could send ordinary material, anything that a neutral nation could sell to countries actively engaged in war.
This question as to the right of the dominions to be strictly neutral is one of the questions yet to be solved, and it will not be solved in the way suggested by my hon. friend.
If that be so, the foreign policy discussed by Mr. Ferguson, Doctor Stewart and others over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation chain is a policy of domestic interest to Canada because, if the Minister of Justice is right-and I believe he is-the right of this country to be neutral in the event of war has not yet been established. Therefore the commitments being made by the national government of Great Britain with European dictators are commitments in which this parliament may find itself involved in the future.
I therefore urge upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government to reconsider any decision they may have taken, to reconsider the statement made last night by the Prime Minister, and not to attempt to muzzle the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in connection with matters of this kind. I want to do more than that; I want to express on behalf of what I am certain is a very large section of our population, our
Radio Broadcasting

appreciation of the manner in which the present corporation is endeavouring to place before the Canadian people the many sides in connection with various problems. I believe that that is appreciated throughout the length and breadth of the country, and I am surprised that a Liberal government in Canada should take an attitude which I regard as distinctly illiberal, and different from the traditional Liberal point of view. After all, those of us who sit in this comer share that traditional viewpoint.

That is his speech. Evidently he was speaking his personal opinion. As for muzzling or attempting to muzzle the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in any way, no action is taken and no action can be taken, except in case of war or emergency. The only law we have on the subject is contained in the bill before us, in a paragraph of section 3 of which power is given to regulate radio in case of war, riots or conditions of grave emergency. The Prime Minister's reference was entirely to paid commentators, and every country in the world. I think, has had its troubles with paid commentators. I know that at least twenty members of the House of Commons have protested vigorously to me against the broadcasts of Boake Carter from the United States, which come in, not over the Canadian broadcasting stations, but direct from the United States stations. They objected on the ground that the broadcasts are most antiBritish. There has also been a great deal of protest against views expressed by our own paid commentators. But paid commentators are in a very different position from my hon. friend when he engages in a series of discussions presenting on the same evening two views of the same subject. Such a discussion, I think-, represents the greatest possible freedom of the air, in that both sides of any question may be presented on the same evening. But to put on the air a paid commentator to present a very biased view on a subject of international importance is something quite different, and it was upon that that the Prime Minister last evening was giving his personal opinion. I think nothing further can be read into his statement, and as far as that goes, the broadcasting corporation has its own legislation which requires it to control the material that goes over the air. The legislation before us permits the government to take over that control only in case of war, riots or grave emergency.

With reference to what the hon. .member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) said, I think he is under a misapprehension. I was not attacking the hon. gentleman's speech on the radio, in fact I did not hear it. I made the statement about Mr. Cordell Hull of my own volition. The hon. gentleman will find the same observations in my address of March 24, and also on the same date the remarks of a member of the British house to the very same effect as to his opinion of this society. I said further that I had often read the speeches of the hon. members for Rosetown-Biggar and Essex East (Mr. Martin) on other subjects with a great deal of interest, but I did not hear these radio addresses. I did object to the policy of the corporation and these debates; I object to it now and I have objected to it all along. And since the remarks made by me on April 28 objecting to this broadcast the government brought down paragraph (d) of section 3 of this bill, a new section which gives the government of the day power to make regulations in case of actual or apprehended war, rebellion, riot or other emergency.
Dealing with the particular principle referred to by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) I may say that he has been a member of the house for only two or three years. He is a gentleman for whom I have some regard, and I would not make an

Radio Broadcasting
unfounded statement concerning him or anyone else, because I back up any statement I make.
Let me come to what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has been saying around the Toronto district. The effect of his words is nothing but pacifism. As a result of the British Broadeasting Corporation's policy with regard to this matter, objection was made to that corporation as I pointed out last evening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). It was made by whom? By the secretary of state for war, Right Hon. Leslie Hore-Belisha, and by the Prime Minister of Great Britain. For what reason? Because of the activities of this society, the League of Nations society. Objection came from Poland, from Germany, from Italy and two or three other countries to what these people were saying on the radio, with the result that the British Prime Minister has brought in the very same provision that is contained in paragraph (d) of section 3 of this bill.
Pacifists, of whom the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is one, have had their day in this country, but it will cost us thirty-six millions for defence this year. I objected last night to this part of the radio corporation's program. Let it be understood that I am not criticizing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or any official connected with them. The corporation was created by the former prime minister, and I am one to give them a show, but I have always objected to these debates on controversial matters. They do not convert anybody. We have had several of them on the radio, and people are getting sick and tired of them; they would rather hear music. I may say to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who purports to represent the younger people, that the young people take more interest in social matters and sports than they do in polities, pacifism, radio debates and that kind of thing. As a consequence of the British Broadcasting Corporation's program of debates of this kind and similar propaganda, the secretary of war, Right Hon. Leslie Hore-Belisha, said Britain was expending hundreds of millions on rearmament.
What has happened since 1921 as a result of trying to bring people together through the League of Nations? The league is dead, and the British Broadcasting Corporation have been instructed by the government of the day along the same line as the Prime Minister indicated here last night. I refer to the words I used on March 24 in connection with the national defence estimates as
proof of what I said last night. The secretary of war in England said that this propaganda through the B.B.C. had hurt recruiting and done the empire untold harm. He objected also to what some of the clergy were saying, and to all this campaign of pacifism. Now see where pacifism has brought the mother country. She faces insult and invasion, all as a result of this policy of disarmament in the old land. The minister of war has had difficulty in getting recruits. He brought the matter up in the House of Commons and told the pacifists in the house that they had had their day. They have had their day in this country, too, and I can say, as I said last night, that we are just where we were a hundred years ago. You have no army, no navy, no armed forces; you are depending on the people of the mother country for your liberty and defence. That attitude seems to be very popular in this house; in almost every question that comes up we are told that we belong to the American continent; and I was glad to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) bring in this paragraph (d) because the minister and the Prime Minister were being blamed unjustly for the broadcasts to which I have referred. I alluded to the matter on April 28, and at the end of the discussion these remarks were made:
Mr. Church: You had better send for a lifesaving station.
Mr. Bennett: Was the consent of the government sought?
Mr. Howe: No.
Mr. Bennett: It was not sought or given?
Mr. Mackenzie King: No, that is right.
I objected then and I object now to this linking us up with pan-American propaganda on such a controversial subject as defence and foreign affairs. It is not in the interest of a united empire. We are not dependent upon the Monroe doctrine and pan-Americanism, we are depending on the British fleet, army and air force and the British people who are now so heavily taxed for Canada and the empire. Facts are facts. I agree with every word that was so ably said the other night by my right hon. leader m Chalmers church as to what we owe to Britain. I was sorry that the press, although it could publish four pages of ballyhoo about hockey, could devote only a few lines to the references made in my leader's speech to this matter of what Britain has done for us and the empire.
I say, as I said last night, that there are thousands of people, intelligent people, in this country who are sick and tired of the

League of Nations society and the pacifist ideas which are spread through the schools as well by this agency. I object to it as a citizen and on behalf of the constituency I represent. This League of Nations society is doing and has done a great deal of damage to rearmament, as it did in England until it was checked by the Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain.
In conclusion, may I say I have nothing but the kindest regard for hon. members in the group on my left. They may have their views, and I respect them, but those views are not mine. I am sent by my constituents to represent them, and I believe that the overwhelming majority of the people of this country is in favour of the policy of England and of rearmament and in favour of putting brakes on the sort of thing we have been hearing from radio speakers and pacifists. Let me remind -the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar -that the British labour party voted 2,250,000 "for" to 262,000 "against" on the question of rearmament, and the support of a policy of putting a brake, in difficult days like these, upon these mischievous broadcasts. Am I not to make any criticism here of what takes place in Russia? These words of the Prime Minister with regard to the commission do seem to be in the nature of a warning or of a threat. I cannot think that any private individual would say things in just this way and confidently expect that nothing further than his own private opinion would bring about the required change of policy. Since when did we in Canada adopt the arbitrary methods that prevail in authoritarian countries? Is it possible that a ukase or declaration can be issued by the Prime Minister as to what public boards are to do? I thought responsibility with regard to these matters lay with the broadcasting corporation. I thought the ultimate responsibility lay with parliament. I did not think it was possible for a prime minister to tell this country what its policies were to be. It comes to that.
It is true this kind of arbitrary action might be considered necessary in times of war, but certainly it should be confined to times of emergency, and should be preceded by a proclamation. We are still, I am glad to think, in comparatively normal times, even if they are difficult times. If I understand anything of the principles underlying democracy, we must preserve the fullest right to freedom of speech even in difficult times and even when considering the very complicated problems confronting the world to-day. With the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) I hope that the statement of the Prime Minister-and it is a statement of the Prime Minister-will be reconsidered; that it will not be regarded as the policy of the government, either with regard to members of this parliament or with regard to the broadcasting corporation.

With what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had to say I am generally in accord. We in this parliament should not let the opinion go abroad to the Canadian people that we are seeking in any manner whatsoever to curtail the fullest possible right on the part of the Canadian people to discuss public matters in any way they see fit. The right of free discussion of public affairs is one of the most sacred rights that we in a democracy enjoy. It is one that men have fought to win, and we must not permit any encroachment upon it. I regard some of the opinions expressed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) as an attempt to insert the thin end of the wedge of repression. If commentators are employed by the broadcasting corporation to comment upon the news of

the world they are employed for the purpose of expressing their opinions as to the significance of international events. They are not employed merely for the purpose of narrating the events; that is done by the press. They are commentators upon international events, and being such it is desirable that they should express their opinions. If they are not to express their own opinions and views, whose views and whose opinions are they to express? Is anyone to be set in authority over them to say to them, " You must not express this opinion "? Here are two men who have been commenting upon the news of the day, and their hours of comment are eagerly awaited by thousands of people from one end of Canada to the other: is it necessary that their opinions or views shall coincide with those of all their listeners? What would be the value of comment of that kind?
If comment is to be of any value it must be a clear and honest expression of viewpoints. What is going to happen to comments of this sort upon the news of the day if after a commentator has expressed an opinion upon some controversial point he knows that on the following Monday on the orders of the day the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is going to rise in his place in this house and say, " I object to that expression of opinion "? Is that going to be conducive to honest expression of views and opinions? I would much rather have inaccuracy than suppression of opinion. If these broadcasts are to have any educational value whatever our commentators must have assurance of the fullest and freest right to express the views that they honestly hold. I do not believe for a moment that either Mr. Ferguson or Doctor Stewart are dishonest men or that they are expressing views that they do not honestly hold.

We had a decision by the Supreme Court, of Canada recently that I think is valued by every Canadian. The decision was to the effect that the right of public discussion of public affairs underlies our whole constitution. That is new ground to be broken by the courts of this land, and it is splendid ground. There are fundamental rights that must be maintained and preserved at all costs; for only by the exercise of these fundamental rights can progress result. We must not stifle free discussion in this house. The section under discussion raises a question which, in my mind, ought to be considered at some stage. The discussion which has been proceeding for some time bears directly upon the point I wish to raise. The whole section is one by which the minister may make regulations. The paragraphs define the kinds of regulations he may prescribe.
In the old original bill the application was to a large extent to ship operations and radio stations including ship stations. The establishment of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the ownership by the Dominion of Canada of a portion of the broadcasting stations have introduced a new feature. I am coming to question the wisdom of operating broadcasting stations through a government corporation. In saying that, I admit frankly that in its original form, patterned somewhat after the British Broadcasting Corporation, there was in the minds of those who fostered the Canadian organization the desire to improve broadcasting conditions. I am under the impression that it was the abuse of broadcasting by advertising agencies which really suggested the move. However, as the years have gone by, we are now facing just the condition indicated by the discussion this afternoon.
I find myself wholly in accord with the member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) when he advocates freedom of speech. Whether that freedom of speech is in the form of public expression, or of the written wTord -through the press, or whether it is through this new medium of radio broadcasting, I am in favour of freedom of speech, and I am opposed to the restriction of freedom of speech. But the limitations on -that freedom in broadcasting ought, in my opinion at least, to be the same as the limitations on the newspapers or on utterances from a public platform, with respect to libellous, seditious and such like utterances, which are controlled by our ordinary criminal law. But by introducing control of the administration of a part of broadcasting, and only a part of it, by a government agency, we introduce at once a very difficult proposition, because while we are in favour of freedom of speech we are then faced with the position which has been stated by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), that a government employee or someone paid out of the taxpayers'

money may advocate views which are distinctly at variance with and do offence to a very large number of taxpayers. It is all very well for the hon. member for Selkirk to argue that a man has the right not only to tell the news but to give his opinion of the news. That is all right if he is doing it at his own expense and under his own agency, whatever that agency may be.

That brings me to my comment upon the principle which is involved in this whole business, that is whether it is advisable for a government agency to administer and operate broadcasting stations. I believe the radio corporation should be limited to a supervision of the technique of broadcasting-wavelengths, licensing, the times at which stations shall operate, and their .power. I think it would be better, in the light of the circumstances that have gradually developed, if broadcasting were in the hands of private corporations.

As I said in my opening remarks, I had come to this view after watching the operations of the radio corporation for a few years. Let me say to the minister this: I think this is the first time I have offered what might be considered criticism of the radio corporation, and I am not now criticizing that corporation. Generally speaking, I believe it has discharged rather difficult duties in a fairly efficient way. I am inclined to the view, although my opinion is not, I think, one of the best, the present radio corporation is an exceptionally able body of men, and they are doing a very fair job. But that does not prevent me from taking exception to some of the policies which are being followed, and I do take definite exception to a government body paying individuals to express opinions upon controversial subjects. We do, for instance, carry
on a debate over the air, and I think that probably is good, if it is very carefully supervised. I think the corporation should know beforehand what is going to be said by the two persons taking contrary sides of a question. Such a debate might be useful on some subjects. I am not taking much exception to that. But to give an individual carte blanche to express his opinion on the news of the day, and to use his half hour, or whatever his time may be, for the dissemination of his own views at the taxpayers' expense is, in my opinion, a wrong use of the radio.

I was coming to. that question, and I might as well deal with it now. There has been a good deal of suggestion, shall I say, that we should be very, very careful about the news which is disseminated to see that nothing is done to disturb other nations. I was in the old country for some time this winter, and the whole of Great Britain and the continent were just seething with bitterness one way or another because of the use that was being made of government broadcasting agencies to attack other countries; for instance, Italy was disseminating in Arabic views that would stir up the Arabs in Palestine, and that was carried to a point where it became quite serious. Germany also has its form of broadcasting propaganda. On the other hand, Germany and Italy charged speakers in Great Britain with giving views contrary to their interests. The controversy became very bitter; but fortunately, so far as Italy and Great Britain are concerned, they met and one of the chief points agreed upon between Mr. Chamberlain and the Italian government was that there must be an abandonment of that form of broadcasting. It only goes to illustrate that care ought to be taken in announcing the news not to make the announcement in a form which is distinctly offensive, and calculatedly so.
As to the ordinary news commentators in Great Britain and the United States-and we get them over the short-wave from other countries-1 think they are excellent, and I have no objection at all to that. It is not difficult for a person trained in newspaper work or in headline work in the newspapers to pick out the important news items and to give them to the public in a fair and true light. That is of the very essence of good newspaper work, as newspaper men will agree; that is, the ability to give a news item without
Radio Broadcasting

colouring it with editorial comment. The same principle should be applied to broadcasting. I can see no objection to that. But I do object to engaging commentators and paying them with public funds to give their own interpretations of the news items. If they wish to do so at their own expense or over private broadcasting stations, that is another matter.
This brings me back to. my main point, whether the time has not arrived when we might well consider the abandonment of the actual administration of broadcasting stations by the government of Canada through this corporation and the turning of them back to private ownership, the corporation, of course, retaining control of what affects the public generally, such matters as wave-lengths, the power of the stations, and matters of that kind, which by the way, of course, are definitely affected by international agreements. I think that this discussion brings quite vividly to the front the need of great care in the exercise of the minister's powers under this section, and the point that we are treading on very dangerous ground when commentators are allowed to use their discretion in commenting upon the news of the day.

subtopic: REVISION OF RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I	admit the accuracy
of the position with respect to a sale. I think that is quite sound and proper. But it does seem to go pretty far to require the man who makes repairs on a radio set to find out at his own risk whether the owner has a licence for it, before he can do any repairs on it.

subtopic: REVISION OF RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I	do not think that
the point raised by the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) should be allowed to pass without at least some comment. There is no doubt that private owners of radio broadcasting stations and others who are opposed to public ownership, have within recent times put up a great barrage against government ownership of radio broadcasting. The point which was emphasized by the hon. member for East Kootenay, as far as I could ascertain, was that it was not right that paid commentators or commentators paid by the government should be engaged to comment upon the news, particularly upon the foreign news. I have listened for quite a long time to these Sunday evening broadcasts by Doctor Stewart, I believe ever since they began. I did not agree with him on all occasions, but it does not follow that because I did not agree with him he was wrong and I was right; the reverse may have been the fact, and even though I did not agree with him, the broadcasts are in my opinion a good thing for the people of Canada.
I should be interested to know what complaints have been made to the minister in regard to these broadcasts. I have heard very few complaints myself. The complaints that were made to-day are merely matters of opinion. The statement was made that the commentator was using his imagination without having the facts, and the person who made that complaint did not bring any

Radio Broadcasting
evidence to show that he had the facts and that the other fellow was using his imagination. If there is anything which would make me more favourable to government ownership of radio broadcasting than I have been, it is that we had a government which, although I do not regard it as very progressive, had engaged commentators of the calibre they have engaged for the purpose of analyzing foreign affairs to the people of Canada.

If the hon. member will
permit-he is confusing the government with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

I assume there is some
connection, and that if they were not acceptable to the government they would not hold their positions very long, I may be wrong in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I believe we can assume
there is some connection. However, I am glad that the hon. member brought the point to my attention. I believe that parliament should consider this matter very carefully before it departs from the principle of public ownership which has been in force since 1932.

Could the minister inform
the committee what length of time these commentators have on the radio each week- the ones who have been particularly referred to this afternoon?
I listen to them occasionally. I would say, fifteen minutes, but if somebody assured me that I was wrong I would accept their statement.
Fifteen minutes each?
No. I think they alternate.

I wonder if some of the hon. members who have been complaining this afternoon about the addresses of these commentators have not slightly overstated the case, if, as has been mentioned by the minister, these commentators occupy the radio for only fifteen minutes a week. If we compare that with the whole length of broadcasting by the corporation in a week, it will be seen that very little time is given for comments on the news of the day. I have heard no complaints from any source as to the comments of the gentlemen referred to. I do not know whether the minister or the department have received any. But I have listened to them for quite a long time, and I have been very much interested in what they say. Although very often I find myself in disagreement with their viewpoints on the news of the day, that does not mean that
they should not be permitted to comment over the radio. Similar facilities are granted over the private stations in the United States, and if private corporations can give comments on news in that country why cannot a public utility do the same thing in Canada? If definite complaints are made with regard to the comments, it would be a different story, but so far nothing specific has been stated in this house by way of objection to what has been said. If there is anything definite I should be interested to hear what it is. So far there has been no real complaint except that comments have been made over the radio. These commentators are not propagandists, as suggested by some hon. members. They do not give their own points of view on questions, but merely interpret as best they can the events of the preceding few days. Knowing some of the opinions of some of these gentlemen who give comments over the radio, I am sure that they do not give their own personal points of view, and I do not believe that they are propagandists. I am sorry that my hon. friend from East Kootenay comes out in opposition to public ownership of radio in Canada. Those who remember the kind of broadcasting we had a few years ago, and1 who note the broadcasting that we have to-day, will have observed the tremendous strides we have made in Canada in the past two or three years. Excellent service is given, and I would say that our broadcasts are far superior to those in the United States.
We get most of it from there.

Some of the main broadcasts do come from the United States, as the leader of the opposition has pointed out; but anyone who has lived in the United States for even a few weeks and who has turned on the radio to get some entertainment knows that one is compelled to listen every few minutes to some form of obnoxious advertising. No one who has had that experience would say for a moment that the broadcasting in Canada is not preferable to the broadcasting in the United States. The moment you tune in on any American station, apart from expensive broadcasts, you are in for a long series of advertisements. I am thankful that we in Canada have not broadcasting of that sort.

It would be inopportune to go at length this afternoon into what I know to be some of the misstatements made over the radio, but I would direct the hon. gentleman's attention to references made by Mr. Ferguson to what he called the Cliveden
Radio Broadcasting

intrigue, when he broadcast throughout Canada that there were meetings at Cliveden, at Lady Astor's house, which brought the government of the United Kingdom under the influence of the ambassador of the Fuehrer of Germany-sayings such as that, which were mere scandal and which started first in foreign propaganda. I could refer to other matters but it is not worth while; it is not worth the time. I simply call attention to this fact, that if extreme propaganda of that kind is to be made freely at public expense, some similar opportunity should be allowed to others to controvert these statements. But such opportunity is not given under present conditions.
Does not the minister think that this is carrying bureaucracy rather too far?
It is a shade further than my right hon. friend went, just a shade.

It is going just a bit too far. In the light of present knowledge, does not the minister think that a man should be able to have his radio repaired without being under the necessity of disclosing to the workman who repairs it whether he has a licence or not? Surely that is carrying bureaucracy too far. Bureaucracy has a great hold in Canada in many directions. I have had occasion in the last few days to look into its application in another department of our activities, in our national parks, and now we are going to apply it to radio. I can understand our going a certain distance in the direction proposed here, but when it is suggested that a workman coming to my house to repair my radio should ascertain whether or not I have a licence-well, the average man would say, "That is none of your business; I have employed you to repair my radio and I am prepared to pay you." But the workman will answer, "The government says that I must inquire whether you have a licence before I can repair your radio, and if you want me to do it you will have to satisfy me that you have a licence." Is not that going too far? I do suggest to the minister that it is going a bit too far and that the section might very well disappear.
Frankly I have always had grave doubts, and I have graver doubts ,to-day, whether it is quite sound to apply the principle in question even to the sale of radio sets. Are we not carrying our powers perhaps beyond our jurisdiction? I put this to the minister, because once more we have the old conflict. The courts have decided that we have jurisdiction, but they have not decided that our jurisdiction extends to the sale of radio sets. That surely is a matter of property and civil

rights. We have no right to fix prices and things of that sort ; they are still within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. I have grave doubts whether we have the power, with respect to the sale of radio sets, to impose this condition, and I certainly have graver doubts with respect to the repairing of radios. When I employ a workman to come and repair my radio, when I go to the telephone and ask that a man be sent around to put in a couple of tubes that are worn out, and he comes and says that before he can do that work he must know whether I have a licence, I think we are going too far. What happens then? Is it his business to be a common informer? Is it within the competence of this parliament to deal with the matter? Is it not a question of purely provincial and local jurisdiction, a question of property and civil rights, a question of contract between the workman and myself? Shall we say that such a contract cannot be enforced unless this condition here proposed is complied with? I submit that it is going too far.

I am told that the only
change here is to embody in the act itself a regulation that has been in effect for many years under the Minister of Marine, and more recently the Minister of Transport. Parliament has decided that the operation of a radio shall be illegal unless a licence has been obtained, and certain penalties are prescribed. I see no great objection to putting this regulation in the act. I do not think it is bureaucracy to use every means to enforce the intent of the radio saot. That is the principle on which we have been collecting radio licence fees from the start. A man can bring a policeman into your house to see whether you are operating a radio without a licence. When dealing with a situation of this kind I do not think that it is going too far to have a regulation of this sort, which has been in effect for many years, embodied in the act. It is not a new departure.

Would it not be better to have the system followed in connection with automobile sales? Every automobile salesman must report to the province when he has made a sale. I do not think we should make radio dealers and repair men collect for the government. It is asking too much, for all they get out of it. If they report the sale that ought to be enough; it is then up to the government to collect the licence fee.

I understood the minister to say some time ago that if those who are on relief are not able to get

Radio Broadcasting
a radio licence they would not be pressed too hard by the department. Must the owner of the machine, no matter whether he is on relief or not, produce a licence before he can get repairs done? What is the department's attitude in such a case?

It is a matter of leniency. We do not change the law; we simply do not apply it to people on relief. Similar leniency would apply in the matter of repairs. For instance in the area in the west known as the drought area the instructions have been not to press the collection of radio licence fees. A similar instruction would go out in that area regarding the production of licences in case of repairs.
Would the same thing apply to people on relief in Calgary, or would they have to be definitely in the drought area?
Definitely in the drought area.

I do not think there is anything very objectionable in this condition. I understand it has been in effect by way of regulation for some time, and I rather applaud the minister for having the courage to put it in the act instead of taking advantage of w'hat is unknown to the members of this committee, doing- it in a more or less underhand way by way of regulation. It has not worked any hardship to me. As owner of a radio set, if I ask a man to come and repair it I know I have to have a licence, and if he asks to see it I ought to be prepared to produce it. I do not think it involves making the mechanic act as a collector, for he does not sell me that licence; all he does is ask if I have it, and if I have not he does not repair the radio. Collecting these radio licence fees is rather difficult because of the difficulty of knowing who has them and who has not.

What are the provisions of the act as to the collection of radio licence fees? As the matter stands there is something very wrong about it. The sale of these licences has been placed to a large extent in the hands of department stores and other large establishments, no doubt for the convenience of the public. But the government have also appointed collectors, who unfortunately seem to be as impotent and helpless in the matter as new-born babes. I do not mean to say there is lack of ability on their part to collect, but apparently they have no power. I know of one such man who has made a dozen calls at one home trying to collect, and has been told by the owner to go-wherever he likes; he does not have to pay a licence fee and he will not until he is
good and ready. Surely that is an absurd situation. If the government is merely making a mock gesture of giving men the right to collect these fees, on a commission basis no doubt, and if they have to call on owners of receiving sets over and over again and have no power to force payment of the licence fee, there is something wrong. I have been told by this collector, who is not very far from me, that he knows for a fact that many people in the vicinity have not paid their licence fees and he has no power to force them to do so.
He should report the case to the department.
Well, I shall ibe glad to point that out to him, but there are collectors in the part of Canada I come from who have the impression that they have no power to make people pay.

I understood the minister to say just now in answer to a question that only people in the drought area in Saskatchewan are exempt from the payment of radio licence fees. Does that not apply to any other part of Canada? I represent a section of Toronto in which many people are on relief. They have not the money for licences. I think if something is granted to people in another part of Canada it should be granted to people in similar circumstances in Toronto. I do not see why people in one part of the country who are on relief through no fault of their own should be charged for a licence or deprived of the pleasure of having a radio while people in another section are favoured.

Of course no one is exempt from the payment of radio licence fees, but there is a general instruction to all those collecting radio licence fees that if the owner of a radio can show that he is on relief, or indigent, whatever that means, and is unable to pay, has no earnings, the demand for payment is not pressed. The reason I mentioned the drought area was that the question asked by the hon. member for Bow River had to do with the drought area. But it applies to all people on relief or indigent, and repairs could be included.

When a licence has been issued for a radio set and a repair man comes and asks to see the licence, how does he know that the licence shown him is for that particular machine? Is there any way he can tell?

No.

A man might borrow his neighbour's licence; they might have one licence for the whole street.
The name and address is on every licence. But if there are two or more radios in the house and one licence is shown there is no way to check that.
It seems to me that a radio is a bit of a luxury, and the question arises whether a man on relief should be encouraged to have it.

In connection with the requirement that anyone repairing a radio must assure himself that the owner has a licence, what about a man who comes in and buys a set of tools from the dealer to fix his own radio? Also what about a radio that is in a house but is not being operated? If I correctly understood what was said last night, if an inspector finds his way into the house and discovers a radio there, he may oblige the owner to obtain a licence even if it is not in operation. We have some radios that are Obsolete; perhaps new ones have been purchased and the old ones have been allowed to remain. I hope a man will not be under obligation to purchase a licence for a radio of that kind.
With regard to the amount of the fee, last night the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked whether the owner of a battery set in a home where there is electric power would pay $2.50, and the minister replied that he would. I do not know what distinction is going to be made with respect to electric power in homes. We have a good many people operating ordinary automobile generators with little windmills and thereby producing electricity which they use to charge their radio batteries and perhaps in other ways. In addition, we have the ordinary 32 volt farm lighting plant, which in some cases also charges the radio batteries. I should like the minister to clear up those three points for me, particularly the question as to what is going to be considered electric power in a home.

Taking the last point first, the case to which my hon. friend refers is a local source of supply for that one home. That would be considered a battery set, and the fee would be $2. The act provides that if the house is connected to a central power station the $2.50 fee will apply.
In connection with a radio in a house but not in use, under the act the presumption is that if the radio is in the house it is in use. If the owner can show to the satisfaction of whoever is handling the matter that the radio
f.Mr. Howe.]
is not in use, of course there would be no fee; but under the act there is the presumption, which I think is fair, that if the radio is in the house it is in use.
What about the repair man?

Under the act, before a radio is repaired, the repair man is required to ask if a licence has been obtained. I do not know that it is necessary for him actually to look at the licence; I suppose it is.
Suppose he sells me half a dozen tubes and I take them home?

That would, I think, be a little different from repairing a radio.
Mr. MULOCIv: Under subsection 2 of section 4 the minister may authorize the imposition of a penalty not exceeding $50 and costs or three months' imprisonment for the violation of any regulation. Under the proposed amendment that would extend to the repairs, and may I point out that a man on relief, could not get his radio repaired, even though the person doing the work did it without charge, without the latter being liable to go to gaol for three months. From what the minister said I know it was not his intention that people on relief should not be allowed to use their radios, and I would suggest that the wording of the amendment be changed.

The question of dealing with . relief recipients is entirely a matter of leniency. There is nothing set out in the law providing that if a man is on relief he does not have to pay his licence fee. I was simply explaining that in the administration of the act our instructions are very strict; that a man on relief is not to be pressed for the collection of a radio fee, and the same thing would apply to the repairing of a radio for a man on relief.
Have you the power to do that?
No, we have not. It is a matter of leniency; we have the power to sue or not to sue.
The law should treat everybody alike.

I would point out that it says a person may not make repairs unless the licence has been obtained. It is the man who makes the repairs who will be responsible for the fine or imprisonment, not the man on relief. The man making the repairs is not protected by that statement.

Radio Broadcasting

If my hon. friend will look at subsection 3 of section 10, he will see this provision, which has been in all radio acts since the inception of licences:
No proceedings shall be taken against any person under this section except by order of the minister.
The minister has to sign personally the complaint, and the minister does not sign complaints against persons on relief.

But that relates only to an offence under that section.
Mr. MULOCIv: That has to do with establishing stations without authority.
Surely the minister does not have to authorize every police prosecution.

Every one. I sign them
personally.
Then I think the minister will be very busy for the rest of the year.

It has always been done in that way. My hon. friend was a member of [DOT]the government which drafted these regulations in the first place, and nothing we are doing here changes them particularly. There is only one very slight change in this act; we are changing the language slightly in order to modernize it, but the only real change arises out of a court case which made the old act unworkable. We are changing it in that respect, but these are all old regulations. Ever since I have been minister I have had to sign an authorization for every prosecution.

There are several new
sections and new definitions and sections revised. You will find that right through.
But, as I pointed out, it is simply transferring the regulations, which were issued under ministerial authority, to the act. Those regulations have always been there.

I have no desire, while
we are on this section, to deal with section 10, subsection 1; but as we come to sections 5, 9, 10 and others throughout the bill, I [DOT]think we shall be able to satisfy the minister that these are not merely enacting things that were in the regulations before. I just do not want to allow his statement to pass without calling attention to that fact.

The minister says these regulations were here before. He must recall the difficulties that attended the creation of this enterprise in the first instance, and the criticism that was always being made. The
hon. member for Comox-Alberni says the government is to be congratulated upon having transferred the regulations to the act, but they are still doing it by regulation. This section authorizes the minister to make regulations; that is what we are dealing with. The section says, "The minister may make regulations," and this is one of the items about which the regulations may be made.
Will the minister submit these two questions to the Department of Justice? 1. Has this parliament power to legislate with respect to the sale and conditions of sale of radios in Ontario? 2. Has this parliament the right to insist upon a repair contractor ascertaining whether or not a licence has been taken out by the owner of the radio upon which he is to work, and to make him liable to a penalty if he fails to do so? I shall not take up the time of the committee beyond this.

I shall be glad so to refer those questions, and in the meantime I would suggest that this paragraph stand.
Paragraph (e) stands.
Paragraphs (f) to (k) inclusive agreed to.
On section 4, paragraph (1).

This is the kind of
paragraph about which, in former times, it was the habit of hon. gentlemen now forming the government to complain. After having provided for special matters and special regulations which may be passed, in paragraphs using most of the letters in the alphabet, the minister then puts in a paragraph covering them all, whether those regulations are or are not contained in the preceding paragraphs.

Opposite it says:	"No
change."

Nothing surprises one so
much in the house in the last few years a3 to see the justification the government puts forward for its conduct by saying, "No change."

speechtext:
We are
keeping what is good.

And then one must turn up Hansard and read the speeches of the present Minister of Justice on those occasions when he said there was much danger; the sacred rights and liberties of the people were being taken from them. Then there were references to the powers of the governor in council, and how that bureaucracy was tightening upon the very lives of. the people, and choking them to death. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move:
To amend section 4 of Bill No. 52, by striking out subsection 2 and substituting therefor the following:
"(2) Any person -who violates any regulation made under this section shall be liable upon summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding $50 and costs or three months imprisonment."

Amendment agreed to.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
Section stands.
On section 5-Station licences.

This section illustrates
as well as if not better than any other the protest I raised, when the bill was first introduced. to the effect that the notes in respect of the different sections are deceptive. The note at the side of this section is in these words:
This is existing section 6 reworded to clarify the intention.
As a matter of fact, the section does not clarify the intention at all. The section in the bill has the same effect as section 6 of the Radiotelegraph Act, with the exception of the added words "operate or have in his possession any radio apparatus at." The effect of those words is to make a radio contained in an automobile subject to licence. I do'not believe the minister would seriously suggest that under the old Radiotelegraph Act there was power to licence a radio in an automobile; yet this very section is designed for that purpose.
No.

The minister says, " No." Why, then, does he put in a proviso exempting the cars of tourists who happen to be in Canada? In the first place, I say that the section in the bill creates a new offence. It had previously been an offence to install or to establish a radio station. Under the bill it becomes an offence to operate or to have in one's possession any radio apparatus. The expression " in any place " in the old section has been changed to " at any place " in the new. The proviso is:
Provided that the governor in council may exempt from the operation of this section any radio apparatus installed in any automobile

or other vehicle temporarily in Canada which is owned by a person who resides outside of Canada in a country which accords a similar privilege to residents of Canada.
Therefore I say that in view of the fact that the section creates a new offence, these notes are deceptive.
Let me show another respect in which they are deceptive. We are told that this is the existing section 6, reworded to clarify the intention. It is reworded to clarify the intention of what? Surely it must be to clarify the intention of the original act, which was passed in 1913, and known as the Radiotelegraph Act. Did any one in the house or the country ever hear of such a thing as a radio being installed in a motor car in the year 1913? Is it conceivable that any House of Commons sitting in 1913 intended in a section of an act then enacted to provide for the installation of radios in automobiles? I say that on every possible ground the information is deceptive and is not in accordance with the facts. I point this out in particular at this time because of what was said last night by the Minister of Transport when I raised the matter.

I assume it was the intention in the original act that radios ought to be licensed. This arises out of Rex v. Gignac, quoted the other day by the hon. member.
Progress reported.
